155.title: Holy days and the saints' calendar
155.hook: a few great feasts are kept like Sundays (the list varies by country)
155.tomorrow: Camp 3 close: a rule of life
155.howItsDone: Catholics go to Mass on Sundays and on their country's holy days of obligation, such as Christmas and All Saints; many also follow the saints' calendar, keeping name days, the feasts of their parish's patron and their own patron saints.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fifty days of Easter, and the alleluia coming back. Your line was longer than lent. A new week, and the last full lesson of this camp.

Open a Catholic calendar, the kind that hangs in a parish hall, and look at any square. There's a name in it. March 19, Joseph. August 15, Mary taken up into heaven. November 1, all the saints at once. A random Tuesday in July still has a name: some bishop, some farmer's daughter, some martyr from a city you've never heard of. Almost no day is empty. And a few squares carry a special mark, because on those days Catholics are asked to go to Mass, even on a Wednesday.
screen: `A NAME IN EVERY SQUARE.` → `A FEW SPECIALLY MARKED.`

segments.voice: Those marked days are holy days of obligation. Catholics are asked to go to Mass every Sunday, and on a handful of great feasts they're asked to do the same, whatever day of the week it falls on, and to rest from unnecessary work where they can. The Church's general law lists ten, among them Christmas, the Epiphany, the Ascension, Mary the Mother of God, the Assumption, Saint Joseph, Peter and Paul, and All Saints. But it lets each country's bishops trim the list or move a feast to the nearest Sunday. In the United States the list is shorter, and some are lifted when they fall right next to a weekend. Ask a Catholic in Ireland or Italy and you'll get a different answer. Then there's everyone else on the calendar. The Church keeps a general calendar of saints for the whole world, and a much longer book, the Roman Martyrology, lists saints and martyrs for every day of the year, often several on a single day. Here's the surprise: a saint's feast is usually kept on the day they died, not the day they were born. The old Latin name for that day is dies natalis, birthday, because the Church thinks of it as their birthday into heaven. So every morning, somewhere, somebody is keeping a birthday for someone who died long ago. Parishes are named for them. Children are named for them. And in some Catholic families, a name day is kept like a second birthday.
screen: `MARKED DAYS: KEPT LIKE A SUNDAY.` · `THE LIST VARIES BY COUNTRY.` · `A SAINT FOR EVERY DAY.` · `THE DAY THEY DIED: A BIRTHDAY.`

segments.voice: Think of today as already belonging to someone who lived a whole life and finished it; any Catholic calendar will tell you whose. Then think of someone you knew who has died, and the day that was theirs. If you pray, ask today's saint to pray for you, or for them; if you don't, simply remember one life with gratitude.
Dies natalis. Latin for birthday, the day a saint died, kept as their birthday into heaven. Today's word.
Your line: every day belongs to someone. Somewhere, a birthday into heaven is being kept. Day one hundred fifty-five is in the book.

156.title: Camp 3 close: a rule of life
156.hook: a morning offering, a decade, the Angelus, an evening look back
156.howItsDone: Many Catholics keep a simple personal rule of life, such as a morning offering, the Angelus at noon, a decade of the rosary and an evening examination of conscience; some make it formal as oblates of a monastery or members of a lay third order.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the marked days on the calendar, and a saint's dies natalis in every square. Your line was every day belongs to someone. Today, the last day of the practices.

Holy water at the door. Knees and bows. The Glory Be, the Creed, the morning offering, the Angelus. The Mass scene by scene, from the Confiteor to the Sanctus to the sending. The rosary, a decade at a time. Seven sacraments. Confession up close, the tabernacle and its red lamp, the monstrance, the holy hour. Advent, ashes, stations, the Triduum and the Exsultet. That's what this camp has handed you since the church door: a first Mass, or a first in years. Nobody does all of that every day. So what do people actually do?
screen: `A WHOLE CAMP OF PRACTICES.` → `FAR TOO MUCH FOR ONE DAY.` → `SO WHAT DO PEOPLE DO?`

segments.voice: They keep a rule of life. Rule sounds strict, but in Latin, regula first meant a straight stick, a ruler, the kind you use to draw a line or measure a wall. A rule of life is a measuring stick for your days, not a cage. One that has lasted was written by Saint Benedict for his monks, and Benedictine monasteries still live by it: hours for prayer, for work, for reading, for meals and for sleep. Near the end, Benedict calls it a little rule for beginners. The man tradition calls the father of Western monks thought he'd written a starter kit. You don't have to be a monk. Plenty of lay Catholics keep a rule, some formally as Benedictine oblates or lay Franciscans or members of other third orders, and many simply on a card in their wallet. The classic small rule looks a lot like this camp. Morning: an offering of the day before the phone. Midday: the Angelus when the noon bell rings, or a single Hail Mary. Somewhere in the day, one decade of the rosary, on a walk or in the car. Night: a slow look back at the day, honest, not harsh. Sunday Mass. Confession now and then. A rule isn't meant to be heroic. It's meant to be small enough to keep on a bad Tuesday, and yours enough that you'll want to. Tomorrow a new camp opens: the text itself, starting with the prayer book Benedict's monks prayed seven times a day.
screen: `REGULA: A STRAIGHT STICK.` · `A LITTLE RULE FOR BEGINNERS.` · `MORNING, NOON, A DECADE, NIGHT.` · `SMALL ENOUGH FOR A BAD TUESDAY.`

segments.voice: From everything this camp offered, choose just three things and write them down: one for the morning, one for the middle of the day, one for night. Make each so small it's almost embarrassing: a sign of the cross, one Hail Mary, one minute looking back. If you pray, offer the three to God; if you don't, choose three small practices of attention instead.
Regula. Latin for a straight stick, a ruler, a small, steady pattern of prayer for each day, a measuring stick, not a cage. Today's word.
Your line: small, daily, mine. Day one hundred fifty-six, and with it, camp three is done.

157.title: How the Psalms work
157.hook: 150 songs of praise, anger, grief and trust, prayed by the Church every day
157.howItsDone: Catholics hear a psalm sung or read at every Mass between the readings, and priests, religious and many lay people pray the psalms daily in the Liturgy of the Hours, at morning, evening and night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, regula, a rule of life, a measuring stick for the day. Your line was small, daily, mine. Today a new camp opens: the text itself.

Somewhere right now it's early morning, and a monk in a cold chapel is singing a psalm. Somewhere else it's evening, and a nurse on her break is reading one on her phone. A priest on a train prays one under his breath. A grieving family hears one read at a funeral. Every single day, all over the world, the Church prays the same book of songs, around the clock. It's the oldest prayer book Christians have, and Jesus prayed from it himself.
screen: `A MONK AT DAWN.` → `A NURSE ON HER BREAK.` → `THE SAME BOOK, EVERY DAY.`

segments.voice: The psalter is the Book of Psalms: a hundred and fifty songs. The word comes from Greek. A psalterion was a stringed instrument, and a psalm was a song sung to plucked strings. In Hebrew the book is called Tehillim, praises. But here's the surprise: a great many aren't cheerful at all. There are more psalms of complaint than of anything else: songs that ask God where he's gone, why the wicked win, how long this will last. Psalms of anger so raw they're hard to read aloud. Psalms of grief, of guilt, of homesickness, of trust in the dark. A fourth-century bishop, Athanasius of Alexandria, wrote that most of scripture speaks to you, but the psalms speak for you, like a mirror of your own heart. Whatever you're feeling, someone already prayed it. One practical thing. The Douay-Rheims follows the old Greek and Latin Bibles, which divide a few psalms differently from the Hebrew, so for most of the book the Douay number is one lower than a modern Bible's. The famous shepherd psalm is Psalm 23 in most Bibles, and Psalm 22 in the Douay. On this path, the Hebrew number comes in brackets. Catholics meet the psalms all the time: one is sung at every Mass between the readings, and the Liturgy of the Hours, the Church's daily prayer, walks through them morning, evening and night. The book ends on one line: "Let every spirit praise the Lord. Alleluia."
screen: `PSALTERION: STRINGS PLUCKED.` · `MORE COMPLAINTS THAN PRAISES.` · `THEY SPEAK FOR YOU.` · `DOUAY NUMBERS: ONE LOWER.`

segments.voice: If there's a Bible nearby, let it fall open near the middle, where the Psalms usually are, and read one verse; if not, pick any number from one to a hundred and fifty to look up later. Then ask one honest question, what am I actually feeling today, tired, grateful, angry, worried, fine, and just name it. If you pray, hold that feeling up to God as it is.
Psalter. The Book of Psalms, a hundred and fifty songs for every feeling, prayed by the Church every day. Today's word.

158.title: Two ways (Psalm 1)
158.hook: a tree planted by running waters, and chaff that blows away
158.howItsDone: Psalm 1 opens the psalter, and Catholics pray it in the Liturgy of the Hours and hear it as a responsorial psalm at Mass; many who begin reading the psalms start here, as at a front door.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the psalter, a hundred and fifty songs. Your line was every feeling has a psalm. Today, the first psalm, the front door of the book.

A dry summer. The lawns go brown and the hills turn to straw, but the trees along the river stay green. From a distance you can see where the water runs, because the trees follow it. Their roots found something the rest of the field can't reach. Now the dust at the edge of a parking lot on a windy day, lifting, scattering, landing nowhere. The first psalm, the one that opens the whole book, sets those two pictures side by side and says: there are two ways to live.
screen: `A GREEN TREE IN A DRY SUMMER.` → `DUST ON A WINDY DAY.` → `TWO WAYS.`

segments.voice: Psalm 1 has no title and no author's name. It stands at the entrance like a sign over a door. In the Douay-Rheims it opens: "Blessed is the man who hath not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the chair of pestilence." Listen to the verbs: walked, stood, sat. A slow slide, from passing by, to stopping, to settling in. Then the other way. That person's will, the Douay says, is in the law of the Lord, "and on his law he shall meditate day and night." The Hebrew word for meditate doesn't mean silent thinking. It means to murmur, to mutter under your breath, the same word used for a dove cooing or a lion growling over its catch. Meditating, in the psalms, is saying the words over and over, half aloud, like chewing. And that person is "like a tree which is planted near the running waters", bearing fruit in its season, its leaf not falling. Notice planted: somebody put it there, on purpose, near the water. Then: "Not so the wicked, not so: but like the dust, which the wind driveth from the face of the earth." In the Hebrew the picture is chaff, the husks blown off the threshing floor; the Latin, and the Douay after it, made it dust. Either way it weighs nothing and has nowhere to land. The psalm doesn't say one way is easy and the other hard. It says one has roots.
screen: `WALKED, STOOD, SAT.` · `MEDITATE: MURMUR IT.` · `A TREE PLANTED BY WATER.` · `DUST THE WIND DRIVES AWAY.`

segments.voice: Stand by water if there's a river, a fountain or even a running tap nearby, or picture a tree on a riverbank, its roots going slowly down toward the water under the ground. Ask where your own roots are drinking from these days: what feeds you, and what just blows through? If you pray, murmur one line under your breath, the way the psalm means, blessed is the man; if you don't, just stay with the tree.
Two ways. The first psalm's choice: a tree with roots near water, or dust with nowhere to land. Today's word.
Your line: roots near water. A tree planted by the water, not dust on the wind. Until tomorrow.

159.title: Sleep in peace (Psalm 4)
159.hook: a psalm for night prayer: in peace I will sleep and I will rest
159.howItsDone: Catholics who pray the Liturgy of the Hours pray Psalm 4 at Night Prayer (Compline) on Saturday nights; for centuries it was part of Compline every night, the Church's last prayer before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two ways, and a tree planted by the water. Your line was roots near water. Today, a psalm for the end of the day.

It's one in the morning. The house is quiet, and your brain isn't. You're replaying a conversation from this afternoon, the thing they said, the thing you should have said back. You rehearse the perfect reply, then rehearse it again. You check the time. You turn the pillow over to the cool side. Long ago, somebody lay awake in a bed like this one, and wrote a song about it. The Church has been singing that song at bedtime for centuries.
screen: `ONE IN THE MORNING.` → `REPLAYING THE CONVERSATION.` → `A SONG FOR THAT BED.`

segments.voice: Psalm 4 is a night psalm. For centuries it was prayed at Compline, the Church's last prayer before sleep, and in today's Liturgy of the Hours it's still there on Saturday nights. It starts in trouble. "When I called upon him, the God of my justice heard me: when I was in distress, thou hast enlarged me." Enlarged: in Hebrew, God made room for me. Distress is a tight place, a narrow corner, and the prayer remembers a time God gave it space. Then the line for everyone lying awake angry. In the Douay-Rheims: "Be angry, and sin not: the things you say in your hearts, be sorry for them upon your beds." It doesn't say don't be angry. It says be angry, and don't let the anger turn into harm. And those speeches you make in your head at one in the morning? The Douay says, be sorry for them upon your beds; the Hebrew says something closer to be still there. Saint Paul quotes the first half of that line to the Ephesians, and adds his own: don't let the sun go down on your anger. The psalm ends with the line the whole night is waiting for: "In peace in the selfsame I will sleep, and I will rest." In the selfsame is an old, hard phrase; it seems to mean at once, or together. Not after everything is fixed. Not after you win the argument. The one praying has the same enemies and the same worries, and still decides to lie down and trust. Sleep, in this psalm, is an act of faith.
screen: `A NIGHT PSALM, PRAYED AT COMPLINE.` · `THOU HAST ENLARGED ME.` · `BE ANGRY, AND SIN NOT.` · `SLEEP AS AN ACT OF TRUST.`

segments.voice: Find tonight's unfinished conversation, the one most likely to keep you up, and don't solve it: say it in your heart, the way the psalm says, and let it be quiet. Then try the line for when the light goes off: in peace I will sleep, and I will rest. If you pray, say it to God; if you don't, let it be a way of putting the day down.
Sleep in peace. The last line of Psalm 4, a night prayer that lies down before everything is fixed. Today's word.
Your line: in peace I will sleep. Tomorrow's arguments can wait for tomorrow. Sleep well.

160.title: What is man (Psalm 8)
160.hook: the stars, and yet God is mindful of us
160.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 8 in the Liturgy of the Hours and hear it at Mass, including on the feast of the Holy Trinity in some years; the Letter to the Hebrews applies its words to Jesus.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a night psalm that lies down before anything is fixed. Your line was in peace I will sleep. Tonight, look up.

A farm road at night, far from any town. The car door shuts, the headlights go off, and someone looks up. There are far too many stars. The Milky Way is a smear of light across the whole sky. All of that, and one person on a patch of gravel with cold hands. Someone once stood under that same sky, without telescopes, without knowing how far away any of it was, and asked the question out loud.
screen: `FAR TOO MANY STARS.` → `ONE PERSON ON THE GRAVEL.`

segments.voice: Psalm 8 opens and closes with nearly the same line, like two hands cupped around it: "O Lord our Lord, how admirable is thy name in the whole earth!" In between, the question. "For I will behold thy heavens, the works of thy fingers: the moon and the stars which thou hast founded." Fingers. Not arms, not great labor: the whole night sky as fingerwork, like embroidery. Then: "What is man that thou art mindful of him? or the son of man that thou visitest him?" The Hebrew word for man here, enosh, has the sense of a frail human, someone mortal and breakable. The question isn't philosophical. It's astonished. Why would the one who made all that bother to remember this? Then the psalm turns the smallness inside out: "Thou hast made him a little less than the angels, thou hast crowned him with glory and honour." One detail: the Hebrew says a little less than elohim, a word that can mean God, or gods, or heavenly beings. The old Greek translators chose angels, the Latin and the Douay followed, and the Letter to the Hebrews quotes it that way about Jesus. The Church reads both: every human being small, and crowned. In 1969 the Apollo 11 astronauts left a small disc on the moon with messages from world leaders, and Pope Paul VI's words on it quoted this psalm. The words went all the way up to the thing the psalm was looking at.
screen: `THE WORK OF THY FINGERS.` · `WHAT IS MAN?` · `A LITTLE LESS THAN THE ANGELS.` · `THE PSALM WENT TO THE MOON.`

segments.voice: If it's night, step outside or go to a window; if it's daytime, close your eyes and remember the darkest, starriest sky you've ever seen. Notice how big it is and how small one person is beside it, without hurrying past, then hold the psalm's other half alongside: small, and still remembered. 161.title: The heavens shew forth (Psalm 18 [19])
161.hook: the sky speaks without words, and the law is sweeter than honey
161.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 18 [19] in the Liturgy of the Hours and hear its second half at Mass, often as the responsorial psalm answering a reading about God's law.

segments.voice: Yesterday, enosh, a frail human under a sky full of stars. Your line was small, and remembered. Today the sky gets a voice, and the week closes.

A sunset over a highway. A driver pulls onto the shoulder and holds up a phone, and the picture comes out flat. The phone goes back in a pocket, and the driver just looks. There aren't any words. And yet it's as if something has been said. A poet in ancient Israel had that same feeling and wrote it down, then did something unexpected: he put the sky and a book side by side.
screen: `A SUNSET ON THE SHOULDER.` → `NO WORDS, BUT SOMETHING SAID.`

segments.voice: Psalm 18 in the Douay, 19 in most Bibles, opens: "The heavens shew forth the glory of God, and the firmament declareth the work of his hands." Shew is the old spelling of show. The firmament is the great dome of the sky; the Hebrew word pictures something hammered flat, like beaten metal. Then: "Day to day uttereth speech, and night to night sheweth knowledge." Each day hands the news to the next, like a relay. And yet: "There are no speeches nor languages, where their voices are not heard." The sky speaks in no language, so everyone on earth can hear it. The sun comes out each morning like a bridegroom from his chamber, rejoicing like a giant to run his way, nothing hidden from its heat. Then, halfway through, the psalm turns to the law of the Lord, God's teaching: it converts souls, gives wisdom to little ones, rejoices hearts. The commandments are "more to be desired than gold and many precious stones: and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb." Why put these together? An old Christian image speaks of two books, creation and scripture. In that picture, the sky shows that there is glory, and the page names whose it is. After both, the psalm ends small and personal, asking to be cleansed of hidden faults, and that the words of the mouth and the thoughts of the heart would be pleasing. This week went from the saints' calendar to a rule of life to the first psalms. Here the sky and the page meet.
screen: `THE SKY HAS NO LANGUAGE.` · `THE SUN RUNS LIKE A BRIDEGROOM.` · `THE LAW, SWEETER THAN HONEY.` · `TWO BOOKS: SKY AND SCRIPTURE.`

segments.voice: Go to a window or step outside and look up for a minute; if you can't, close your eyes and remember a sky you've seen. Don't describe it: notice the light, the color, how far it goes, and let it speak without words. If you pray, end with the psalm's first line, the heavens shew forth the glory of God; if you don't, let the sky be enough.
